extractedItems.title: Identifying Immovable Obstructions
extractedItems.question: Which of the following is an example of an immovable obstruction where you may get free relief on the course?

choices.text: A path with an artificial surface
A pile of natural leaves
A divot in the fairway
A mole hill

extractedItems.explanation: Paths with artificial surfaces are considered immovable obstructions. You are allowed free relief from them.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage boy golfer stands near a paved golf cart path with his golf ball next to it, preparing to drop the ball away from the path.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Teen boy golfer next to an artificial surfaced path, about to take free relief.

extractedItems.title: Free Relief from Temporary Water
extractedItems.question: What must you see in order to get free relief from 'temporary water' on the course?

choices.text: You must be able to see water when you take your stance
You must see water anywhere near your ball
There must have been rain earlier in the day
You must hear the sound of water under your feet

extractedItems.explanation: Temporary water is only considered when you can physically see water when taking your stance.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl golfer taking her stance over her ball on the fairway, with a visible puddle of water under her feet.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Teen girl golfer with water showing at her feet as she addresses the ball.

extractedItems.title: Recognising Ground Under Repair
extractedItems.question: Which situation would usually be marked as 'ground under repair'?

choices.text: A blue-marked area with piles of grass cuttings
A patch of bare dirt with no signs
A bunker filled with sand
A wet patch after rain

extractedItems.explanation: Areas with blue stakes or marked in blue with piled up grass or maintenance work are considered ground under repair.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teen boy golfer stands by an area surrounded by blue stakes, with some grass cuttings piled up inside the marked area.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Teen golfer next to blue-staked ground under repair with grass piles.

extractedItems.title: What Kind of Animal Holes Give Free Relief?
extractedItems.question: Which of these animal holes lets you get free relief according to the rules?

choices.text: A mole hill
Worm holes
An insect burrow
A divot made by another player

extractedItems.explanation: Mole hills and holes made by animals like moles, mice or rabbits give you free relief. Worms and insects do not count.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teen girl golfer stands near her ball, which is next to a mole hill on the edge of the fairway.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Teenage girl golfer and golf ball by a fresh mole hill.

extractedItems.title: When Is Free Relief Allowed for Abnormal Course Conditions?
extractedItems.question: In which situation can you take free relief from an abnormal course condition?

choices.text: The ball is lying in temporary water
Your stance would be on a mole hill
You are distracted by the view of a path far away
Your swing is interfered with by an immovable obstruction

extractedItems.explanation: You get free relief if your ball, stance, or swing is interfered with by abnormal course conditions. Visual distraction alone doesn't count.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teen boy golfer preparing to hit a shot but his feet and club are near a visible puddle and a mole hill, with an artificial path crossing his swing path.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Teen golfer with stance on mole hill and a puddle, artificial path close to swing.

reviewedItems.title: Identifying Immovable Obstructions
reviewedItems.question: Which of the following is considered an immovable obstruction, entitling you to free relief under the Rules?

choices.text: A path with an artificial (man-made) surface
A pile of leaves gathered by the wind
A divot hole in the fairway
A mole hill

reviewedItems.explanation: A path with a man-made surface is classed as an immovable obstruction. You are allowed free relief from it. The other options are either loose impediments, natural damage, or animal holes.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl golfer stands next to a paved pathway on the fairway, her ball lying beside it as she prepares to drop the ball for free relief.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: Teen girl golfer next to an artificial-path taking free relief.

reviewedItems.title: Free Relief from Temporary Water
reviewedItems.question: When can you take free relief for temporary water on the course?

choices.text: You can see water on the ground under your feet or the ball when taking your stance
You notice water in a nearby ditch
It has rained at some point earlier that day
You hear squelching under your shoes

reviewedItems.explanation: You must be able to see water physically under your feet or the ball when taking your stance for it to be temporary water. Just dampness, sound, or distant puddles aren't enough.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl golfer taking her stance over her ball on the fairway, with a puddle of water visible under her shoes and ball.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: Teen girl golfer with water visible at her feet as she addresses the golf ball.

reviewedItems.title: Recognising Ground Under Repair
reviewedItems.question: Which area is most likely to be marked as 'ground under repair' where you may get relief?

choices.text: A blue-marked area with piles of grass cuttings
A patch of bare earth not marked by anything
A normal bunker filled with sand
A spot of wet grass after rain

reviewedItems.explanation: Ground under repair is usually marked with lines or stakes (commonly blue or white) and can include areas with piled grass from maintenance.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teen boy golfer is next to an area surrounded by blue stakes containing grass cuttings, identifying ground under repair.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: Teen golfer beside marked ground under repair with piles of grass.

reviewedItems.title: What Kind of Animal Holes Give Free Relief?
reviewedItems.question: For which of these is free relief generally given if it interferes with your ball or stance?

choices.text: A mole hill
Worm casts
An insect nest
A divot made by a golf shot

reviewedItems.explanation: Holes or hills made by burrowing animals such as moles, rabbits, or similar, entitle you to relief. Worms, insects, and divots do not qualify.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl golfer in the fairway with her ball lying next to a clear mole hill, illustrating animal hole relief.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: Teen girl golfer and her golf ball next to a fresh mole hill.

reviewedItems.title: When Is Free Relief Allowed for Abnormal Course Conditions?
reviewedItems.question: In which of these situations are you allowed to take free relief for an abnormal course condition?

choices.text: Your ball is lying in temporary water
Your stance would be on a mole hill
You are distracted by the sight of a path a long way off
Your swing is physically interfered with by an immovable obstruction

reviewedItems.explanation: Free relief is allowed if your play is physically interfered with by temporary water, an animal hole, or an immovable obstruction. Mere distraction, such as seeing a path in the distance, does not qualify.
reviewedItems.imagePrompt: A teen boy golfer on the fairway, with his feet on a mole hill and near a puddle, and an artificial path close to his swing.
reviewedItems.imageAlt: Teen golfer with stance on mole hill, puddle, and artificial path interfering.
